hints: Start with Fig. 1.2 - look closely at the top edge of tissue A. What tiny hair-like projections can you see, and what type of lining tissue in the airways has those?
Tissue B forms a continuous band just under the lining. Think about which tissue can contract to narrow the airway diameter during ventilation control.
Tissue D contains large rounded cells sitting in spaces within a solid matrix. Think about which firm but flexible supporting tissue keeps larger airways open.
walkthrough:
Reading Tissue A From The High-Power View**
Fig. 1.2 shows tissue A at high power. You can see a row of cells with dark nuclei at the base and fine hair-like cilia projecting from the top surface. That combination is the classic ciliated epithelium that lines the bronchi and bronchioles.

Identifying The Contractile Layer B**
In Fig. 1.1, B is a smooth band running just outside the epithelium all around the airway. This position and smooth appearance fits smooth muscle, which contracts or relaxes to change airway diameter and control airflow.

Recognising The Supporting Tissue D**
D is a thick plate with chondrocytes in lacunae embedded in matrix. That is cartilage. It provides firm support to prevent collapse of the airway while still allowing some flexibility.
Final answer: A - ciliated epithelium / epithelial tissue; B - smooth muscle; D - cartilage.

hints: Think about what small glands in the bronchial wall add to the airway surface - what sticky secretion coats the lining?
Imagine dust, pollen or bacteria breathed in and landing on that sticky layer - what happens to them next?
Link the sticky layer to the cilia you saw in Fig. 1.2 - in which direction is material moved, and why does this protect the alveoli?
walkthrough:
Secreting A Protective Mucus Layer**
Glands labelled C produce and release mucus / mucin onto the airway surface. The mucus spreads to form a continuous layer over the ciliated epithelium.

Trapping Inhaled Particles And Microbes**
Mucus is sticky, so it traps bacteria, viruses, dust, pollen and fungal spores from inhaled air. This acts as a barrier and stops pathogens reaching the delicate epithelial cells and the gas exchange surface in the alveoli.

Removing Mucus By The Ciliary Escalator**
Cilia on tissue A beat in a coordinated way to move the mucus layer up and away from the alveoli and lungs towards the back of the mouth, where it can be swallowed. This constantly clears trapped material and keeps the airways healthy.

Final answer: Glands C secrete mucus which forms a layer over the ciliated epithelium. Mucus traps bacteria, viruses, dust and pollen and prevents pathogens reaching alveoli. Cilia move mucus away from lungs toward mouth to be swallowed.

hints: Find $4.0 \text{ kPa}$ on the x-axis of Fig. 1.3, go straight up to meet the dashed curve for pH 7.7 and the solid curve for pH 7.4, then read across to the y-axis.
walkthrough:
Reading Both Curves At The Same pO2**
Line up $pO_2 = 4.0 \text{ kPa}$ on the x-axis. Move vertically up to the dashed pH 7.7 curve and read about $72\%$ on the y-axis. Move up to the solid pH 7.4 curve at the same $pO_2$ and read about $60\%$. Always include % for saturation.
Final answer: At $pO_2$ of $4.0 \text{ kPa}$: pH 7.7 = 72% saturation; pH 7.4 = 60% saturation.

hints: Hyperventilation lowers $pCO_2$ and raises blood pH to 7.7. Look at Fig. 1.3 - does the dashed pH 7.7 curve lie to the left or right of the normal pH 7.4 curve?

At tissue $pO_2$ values of about $2-6 \text{ kPa}$, haemoglobin stays more saturated on the left-shifted curve. Think about what higher saturation means for how much oxygen is let go to respiring cells.
walkthrough:
Linking Hyperventilation To Higher Affinity**
Hyperventilation washes out $CO_2$, so blood pH rises to 7.7. Fig. 1.3 shows the oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the left at pH 7.7. A left shift means haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen and holds onto it more tightly.

Explaining Reduced Delivery To Tissues**
In respiring tissues where $pO_2$ is low, about $2-6 \text{ kPa}$, haemoglobin is still highly saturated on the pH 7.7 curve, for example $72\%$ versus $60\%$ at $4.0 \text{ kPa}$. Because less oxygen dissociates from haemoglobin, the supply of oxygen released to respiring tissues decreases.

Final answer: Hyperventilation decreases oxygen supply to respiring tissues. At higher pH haemoglobin has higher affinity for oxygen and remains more saturated, so less oxygen dissociates / is released in tissues, e.g. 72% vs 60% saturated at $4.0 \text{ kPa}$ $pO_2$.
